messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Anh was thirty-two when it happened, working as a staff accountant at a mid-sized logistics firm in Orange County. He had emigrated from Vietnam as a child, built a quiet life — a marriage, a house, a routine of spreadsheets and quarterly reports — and he had never imagined that a business trip to a satellite office in a Central American country would end with armed men dragging him from a hotel parking lot. For seventy-two hours, they kept him in a concrete room, asking questions he could not answer about shipments he had never authorised. They burned the soles of his feet with a soldering iron. They video-recorded his pleas and played them back as a loop on a laptop propped against the wall. He remembers the smell of his own skin and the way one guard kept humming a pop song he had heard on a local radio station. He remembers begging, offering money he did not have, trying to explain that he was just an accountant, just a spreadsheet man. They did not believe him. When he was finally released — dumped outside a police station at three in the morning, still wearing the singed suit trousers — he called his wife, but the words came out wrong, and she thought he was joking.

Back in the United States, the memory did not arrive as a coherent story. It came as a film that played over and over, but the scenes were always in the wrong order: the pop song before the burning, the laptop before the parking lot. Sometimes the memory felt as though it belonged to someone else, a stranger he had watched in a movie — the man on his knees was not him, could not be him. He had come to believe that the torture had permanently changed something inside him, that he was now the kind of person this could happen to, and that was worse than the physical scars. He became certain, too, that another person — someone braver, more resourceful — would have found a way to stop the event. A smarter man would have talked his way out, would have convinced the guards he was not worth their time. That Anh had not even tried to escape, that he had simply screamed and cried and given them his wife’s phone number, proved to him that he had always been weak.

At work, the triggers surfaced in unexpected places. Talking to a stranger — a delivery driver at the office, a new client on the phone — made his throat close, because you could never know who would harm you. The guard who had hummed the pop song had been friendly at first, had offered him water. Strangers now carried that same mask of casual danger. More disabling was the impossibility of discussing the future. When his boss asked about next quarter's projections, or when colleagues planned team outings months ahead, Anh felt a violent confusion: the concept of a future had become thin, abstract, almost offensive. After torture, the future was a thing that had been taken from him; talking about it felt like pretending the room had never existed. He began to decline meetings that involved long-term forecasting. He started eating lunch alone at his desk, wearing headphones so that he did not have to hear small talk from strangers in the breakroom.

His wife found him one night staring at the sliding glass door, certain that someone was about to kick it in. She asked why he would not talk about their summer vacation plans. He could not explain that the word *vacation* sounded like a sick joke. The divorce was final six months later. She said he had become a different man, and he agreed with her. He had permanently changed for the worse, and the evidence was everywhere: the way he flinched at the mail slot, the way he could not watch movies with violence, the way he had stopped returning calls from his own brother.

What finally brought him to a clinic was a panic attack in the middle of a client presentation. A partner in the firm had asked him to walk through a five-year budget forecast. Anh opened his mouth, saw the whiteboard, and saw instead the white wall of the concrete room. He excused himself, locked himself in a bathroom stall, and wept — not from sadness but from a profound sense that he was living inside someone else’s memory. That night, he searched online for a therapist who specialised in trauma, because he was afraid that if he did not, the film would never stop playing, and he would lose his job, his apartment, the last thread of a life that no longer felt like his own. He was most afraid, he told the intake coordinator, of being asked to talk about the future. But he also hoped, for the first time in three years, that maybe a stranger would be able to help.
